title: The great foundations
hookLine: the long satipatthana, with the four truths expanded

cards: Open the Pali canon in two places and you find nearly the same teaching twice. The teaching on the four foundations of mindfulness has one home in the Middle-Length Discourses, and this path met it there.
It has another here, in the twenty-second Long Discourse. For long stretches the two read alike. Then the long one keeps going where the short one moves on, and it's longer for one reason.

teach.h: THE DIRECT PATH, AMONG THE KURUS.
teach.b: It's the Mahasatipatthana Sutta, the great discourse on the foundations of mindfulness.

It opens among the Kurus with a bold line: this is the direct path for the purification of beings, for overcoming sorrow and lament, for the ending of pain and grief, for realizing nibbana. Namely, the four foundations.

Body: the breath, the postures, clear awareness in every action, the parts of the body, the elements, the charnel ground. Feelings: pleasant, painful, neither. Mind: with greed or without, with hate or without.

teach.h: THE FOUR TRUTHS, SLOWED RIGHT DOWN.
teach.b: And mental qualities: the hindrances, the heaps, the senses, the factors of awakening, and the four noble truths. And here the long version slows right down. What is the truth of suffering?
Birth, aging, death, sorrow, lament, pain, grief, despair, and each word is defined. Where does craving arise?

Wherever something in the world seems pleasant and agreeable: the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, the mind, and then sights, sounds, smells, contacts, feelings, thoughts, one by one. Where does it cease?
In exactly the same places. That repetition is the point. The long way doesn't add new ideas.

It walks the same ground slowly enough that you can see craving start and stop in the most ordinary places. And at the end, a promise that shrinks. Whoever practices these four for seven years can expect a fruit.

teach.h: SEVEN YEARS, DOWN TO SEVEN DAYS.
teach.b: Never mind seven years: six, five, four, all the way down.
Never mind a year: seven months, down to half a month. Never mind that: seven days.

how: In Myanmar, Sri Lanka and Thailand the Mahasatipatthana Sutta is often chanted in full, sometimes at the bedside of the dying, and a number of modern meditation methods trace themselves to it.

games.q: the great foundations: tap the pairs.

s: DN 22 adds new practices that MN 10 doesn't have
its main addition is a fuller unfolding of the four noble truths.
the sutta says craving ceases in the same places where it arises
the eye, the ear, sights, sounds and so on, one by one.
the promised fruit needs at least seven years
the Buddha shortens it step by step, all the way to seven days.

games.q: the Buddha promises a fruit to whoever practices the four foundations. for how long do they need to practice?
o: seven years, then he shortens it all the way to seven days.
only monks can expect a fruit.
games.why: seven years, then six, five, down to one; then seven months; and at last, seven days.

practice: Walk the four foundations once, slowly: feel the body sitting and the breath moving; ask whether this moment is pleasant, unpleasant or neither; then whether the mind is calm or restless, wanting or not; then whether a hindrance is here, or something like interest or ease.
Then back to the body, and around again. If you have time, keep going, up to fifteen minutes.

wordCard.voice: Satipatthana. The Mahasatipatthana Sutta: the four foundations of mindfulness, with the four noble truths unfolded step by step. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali satipatthana: sati, mindfulness; patthana or upatthana, foundation or establishing.

carryVoice: Your line: the long way. The same ground, walked slowly enough to see. That's day five hundred fifty-five.
